subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]
passage: Sunday night. Diary, my quiz plan is going well. Every day at breakfast I read the newspaper's page for children, and at night I read a chapter of my general knowledge book. Each time I find something new, I write it in a small blue notebook: places, people, records. Today I wrote that the tallest waterfall is in South America, and that a famous marathon runner comes from Kenya. It's fun, like collecting stamps. Mehak tested me at lunch and I got seven right out of ten. I want to read the sports page too tomorrow. Vidya.

qa.q: Where does Vidya write new facts?
qa.a: Vidya writes new facts in a small blue notebook.

qa.q: Why does Vidya say the reading feels like collecting stamps?
qa.a: Vidya finds each new fact enjoyable and worth keeping, which shows a happy and curious mood.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vidya add, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could practise with a partner using mock rounds. Reading adds facts, but answering questions aloud shows what has really stuck.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Vidya's preparation?
qa.a: Mehak tested Vidya at lunch and saw seven out of ten right, so Mehak probably sees steady progress and may feel encouraged too.

grounding: A girl reads the newspaper's page for children each day and a general knowledge book at night, and keeps a notebook of new facts.

subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]
passage: Every morning in Sunaina's small town near Nashik, the newspaper boy, Ramesh, threw the paper onto the verandah at six. By six-fifteen Sunaina had opened it to the children's page. She read it while her mother made tea: a new bird found in the hills, the longest river in Africa, a record for the tallest sandcastle. At night, under the tube light, she read one chapter from a thick general knowledge book borrowed from the town library. Anything new went into a green notebook with three columns: Places, People, Records. By the quiz, the notebook had forty pages. Ramesh started throwing the paper more gently, so the children's page wouldn't tear.

qa.q: What were the three columns in Sunaina's notebook?
What does Sunaina opening the paper by six-fifteen suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She is eager and curious, and enjoys the daily reading rather than seeing it as a chore.

qa.q: What else could Sunaina add to her reading plan, and why?
qa.a: She could test herself weekly from the notebook, because reading adds facts but testing shows which ones stick.

qa.q: How does Sunaina's routine look to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh notices how much she values the paper and starts throwing it gently, so he seems touched and supportive.

grounding: It shows a girl reading the children's page daily and a general knowledge book at night, keeping a notebook of new facts.

subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]
passage: Dalia lived in a flat above a bakery in Lisbon, and her quiz team had six weeks until the city schools' competition. Every morning she read the children's section of the free newspaper at breakfast. Every night she read five pages of an old book of world facts that her grandmother had kept. Anything she didn't know went into a small notebook with a pencil tied to it. By the second week, her friend Marek was quizzing her on the bus. "Highest waterfall?" "Angel Falls, Venezuela." "Smallest country?" "Vatican City." By the fifth week the notebook was nearly full and Marek was sulking because he couldn't catch her out.

qa.q: What was tied to Dalia's notebook?
qa.a: A pencil was tied to it.

qa.q: How did Marek feel by the fifth week?
qa.a: Marek was sulking, a bit frustrated that he couldn't catch Dalia out any more.

qa.q: What else could Dalia add to her reading, and why?
qa.a: She could practise answering under time pressure, because reading builds knowledge but quizzes also need speed.

qa.q: How does the steady reading look to Marek?
qa.a: Marek enjoys the bus quizzes at first, but as Dalia gets better he sees how much the daily reading has paid off.

grounding: It shows a girl reading a newspaper's children's section daily and a facts book at night, keeping a notebook of new facts.
